nameStory: Eastern teaberry earned its name because early colonists brewed its leaves into a refreshing tea that tastes like wintergreen. The plant is also called checkerberry for its bright red berries that dot the forest floor like game pieces, and wintergreen because it stays green all winter long when most other plants have lost their leaves.
description: Eastern teaberry is a low-growing evergreen shrub that creeps along the forest floor, rarely reaching more than 6 inches tall. It has glossy, oval leaves that grow in small clusters and produces tiny white bell-shaped flowers in summer, followed by bright red berries. This hardy little plant forms patches by spreading underground, creating carpets of shiny green leaves beneath taller trees.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, leathery oval leaves with a glossy shine, about 1-2 inches long. Crush a leaf and smell the unmistakable wintergreen scent - like mint toothpaste or candy canes.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Stays very low to the ground, usually under 6 inches tall, spreading by underground runners to form small colonies. Stems are often hidden beneath the leaves.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white or pinkish bell-shaped flowers that nod downward, blooming in midsummer. They're easy to miss tucked beneath the leaves.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright red berries about the size of a pea that persist through winter. They're actually dry capsules that look and feel like berries, with a wintergreen flavor.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems are green to reddish, while older stems develop thin, papery bark that peels slightly. The stems feel somewhat woody despite the plant's small size.

habitat: Look for eastern teaberry in acidic soils under coniferous and mixed forests, especially where pines, hemlocks, and oaks grow. It thrives in well-drained, sandy or rocky soils and is common on woodland slopes and forest edges throughout New England's hills and mountains.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green and tender, while old berries from the previous year may still be visible. The wintergreen scent is strongest in fresh spring growth.
seasonality.summer: Small white bell flowers appear in July, hanging beneath the mature glossy leaves. This is when the plant is most easily spotted due to the contrast of flowers against dark green foliage.
seasonality.fall: Bright red berries ripen and become prominent as other forest plants lose their leaves. The evergreen foliage may take on slightly reddish tints in cold weather.
seasonality.winter: One of the few green plants visible in snowy forests, with glossy leaves and persistent red berries creating striking color against white snow. The leaves may appear more bronze or reddish in cold weather.

funFact: The wintergreen flavor in teaberry comes from the same chemical compound (methyl salicylate) found in aspirin - in fact, this plant was once harvested commercially to make both wintergreen flavoring and pain relief medicine before synthetic versions were developed.
confusionNotes: The only other wintergreen in New England is creeping snowberry, but it has much smaller white berries and tiny round leaves. Remember: teaberry has RED berries and bigger oval leaves, while snowberry has WHITE berries and tiny round leaves.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this "wintergreen" plant with wintergreen essential oil sold in stores today - most commercial wintergreen flavoring now comes from black birch bark or is made synthetically, not from actual teaberry plants.
compareHints: Eastern teaberry is much larger and more robust than its relative creeping snowberry, with leaves 3-4 times bigger and bright red berries instead of white ones. Teaberry grows in small upright clusters while snowberry truly creeps along the ground with trailing stems, and teaberry's wintergreen scent is much stronger when leaves are crushed.

relatedSpecies.distinction: While eastern teaberry grows 3-6 inches tall with upright stems and larger leaves, creeping snowberry hugs the ground with much smaller leaves and a truly prostrate growth habit.
